summary: The participant is a Chiang Mai resident and event emcee who seeks experiences both for personal enjoyment and to explain local culture and tourism to foreign visitors. Temple visits reliably provide the relaxation, prayer, and photography outcomes they want. By contrast, a Facebook-promoted Japanese festival promised Japanese culture and activities but felt primarily like a food festival with contemporary performances, leading the participant to leave within an hour and regard the visit as wasted time. That mismatch reduced their trust in event promotion and made them more selective, with attendance around once a month considered sufficient. They now reject events using AI-generated promotional images, read social-media feedback, and sometimes ask a trusted friend to attend first and report back privately through LINE. Some friends reportedly share the same uncertainty about whether promoted events will match reality. The central decision implication is that the observed need is not broader event discovery alone, but low-effort, credible evidence that an experience is authentic and matches its promotion before someone commits limited time.
top_pains: Event promotion can promise culture, lifestyle, and learning while the actual event primarily offers food or generic entertainment.
The Japanese festival's performances felt contemporary rather than representative of the everyday life or authentic culture the participant expected.
A disappointing event costs scarce personal time; the participant concluded they should not have spent time there.

AI-generated promotional images are treated as an immediate signal that the real experience will not resemble the advertisement.
Real photographs still may not provide enough confidence, requiring additional verification from another person.
The participant relies on a friend to assume the risk of attending first, creating a slow and socially costly workaround.
Work limits the participant's ability to try desired experiences such as a homestay.
Without first-hand experiences, the participant lacks the tourist perspective they want for telling useful, credible stories in their work.

The participant can answer some visitors' questions after events but cannot answer everything, and the information appears distributed across websites, Facebook groups, physical places, and personal knowledge.
key_facts: The participant visits Chiang Mai temples for relaxation, prayer, and photography.
Temple visits consistently meet expectations by providing peace and opportunities to take beautiful pictures.
The disappointing Japanese festival occurred about a year before the interview.
The participant discovered the Japanese festival through a Facebook promotion viewed on their phone.
The promotion described Japanese culture and activities that would help attendees learn more about Japan.
The participant expected authentic Japanese lifestyle, history, culture, and ways of life.
At the event, the participant encountered what they characterized as a food festival with performances rather than the promised depth of cultural experience.
After seeing enough, the participant left; the total time involved was described as not more than one hour.
Following that experience, the participant began asking friends whether they had already attended uncertain events.
The participant may tell a friend they are busy, ask the friend to go first, and later request a one-to-one report through LINE.
The participant uses friends with similar interests or perspectives as trusted proxies for judging whether an event is worth attending.
The participant does not attend many events, describes themselves as selective, and considers approximately one event per month acceptable.
The participant first filters events by personal interest, then assesses whether the promotion is trustworthy.
They will not attend when the promotional post or image appears AI-generated.
When promotions contain real images but remain uncertain, they may ask a friend to verify the experience first.
They also read feedback posted by other people on social media before deciding.
The participant said some friends have the same problem of looking at event promotions and remaining unsure.
Although personally introverted, the participant's emcee work requires speaking with tourists and presenting information in English.
The participant reports sufficient opportunities to meet nomads in daily life and is willing to approach them when there is something specific they want to learn.
A homestay is a desired future experience because the participant wants to understand the tourist experience and use it to tell tourists better stories about Chiang Mai.
The homestay has not happened because the participant is still working and does not have time.
In their emcee role, the participant adds origin, village, and cultural stories to product presentations rather than only helping sell products.
Audience members sometimes approach the participant after performances for more information.
The participant shares knowledge directly and may point people toward a website, Facebook group, phone contact, or physical location.

unanswered_questions: When was the participant's most recent event-selection decision, and did they attend, decline, or ask someone else to verify it?
How often does misleading promotion cause the participant to skip an event, leave early, or send a friend first?
What exact evidence makes an event feel authentic: attendee photographs, unedited video, organizer identity, detailed schedules, reviews, or recommendations from known people?
How does the participant determine whether an image is AI-generated, and how often might this rule reject legitimate events?
How recent must reviews or friend reports be to remain useful for a recurring or changing event?
Would the participant trust reports from verified strangers, or only from friends with similar interests and expectations?
What burden or consequence does asking friends to attend first create for those friends or for the relationship?
Which event categories besides cultural festivals produce the same expectation gap?
How much travel time, admission cost, or schedule disruption is the participant willing to risk for an unverified event?
How important is solving event trust compared with the participant's larger constraint of limited time from work?
What format would best help the participant reuse first-hand experiences in their emcee work: structured notes, bilingual summaries, source links, photos, audio, or video?
Beyond some friends, which residents, tourists, introverts, or time-constrained workers avoid events because they cannot verify promotional claims?
opportunity: A bounded hypothesis is that selective, time-constrained event seekers may value a lightweight credibility layer showing recent, real attendee evidence and a clear comparison between advertised and actual experiences. This could reduce dependence on sending trusted friends first while helping the participant identify culturally substantive events. The interview supports the behavior and workaround, but does not establish demand for a new product or willingness to contribute, trust, or pay.
next_step: Recruit the participant and four to six similarly selective Chiang Mai residents from their friend network. Show them five real event listings augmented only with recent attendee photos, a short "promised versus experienced" note, and source identity, then compare their attend-or-skip decisions and confidence with the original Facebook listings. Useful validation would be repeated decisions made without contacting a friend, accompanied by participants correctly explaining which evidence changed their confidence; absence of that behavior would weaken the hypothesis.

After seeing enough, the participant left; the total time involved was described as not more than one hour.
Following that experience, the participant began asking friends whether they had already attended uncertain events.
The participant may tell a friend they are busy, ask the friend to go first, and later request a one-to-one report through LINE.
The participant uses friends with similar interests or perspectives as trusted proxies for judging whether an event is worth attending.
The participant does not attend many events, describes themselves as selective, and considers approximately one event per month acceptable.
The participant first filters events by personal interest, then assesses whether the promotion is trustworthy.
They will not attend when the promotional post or image appears AI-generated.
When promotions contain real images but remain uncertain, they may ask a friend to verify the experience first.
They also read feedback posted by other people on social media before deciding.
The participant said some friends have the same problem of looking at event promotions and remaining unsure.
Although personally introverted, the participant's emcee work requires speaking with tourists and presenting information in English.
The participant reports sufficient opportunities to meet nomads in daily life and is willing to approach them when there is something specific they want to learn.
A homestay is a desired future experience because the participant wants to understand the tourist experience and use it to tell tourists better stories about Chiang Mai.
The homestay has not happened because the participant is still working and does not have time.

Audience members sometimes approach the participant after performances for more information.

A bounded hypothesis is that selective, time-constrained event seekers may value a lightweight credibility layer showing recent, real attendee evidence and a clear comparison between advertised and actual experiences. This could reduce dependence on sending trusted friends first while helping the participant identify culturally substantive events. The interview supports the behavior and workaround, but does not establish demand for a new product or willingness to contribute, trust, or pay.
